text.title: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
text.body_text: Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures. All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
text.summary: A series of strikes have hit Belgium in recent months as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs.
text.alt_text: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike — BBC News - World

text.title: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie
text.body_text: “Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie.
text.summary: The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy “Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here. In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. With the coin-flip and a roll of the personal globe, Akeem and his sidekick Semmi go to America but more specifically Queens because where else would be more fitting to find his bride? While trying to assimilate to the fast pace of New York living, he pursues Lisa, the heiress to a different kind of throne – that of a fast-food business called McDowell’s. The problem is, she’s already engaged to another. Akeem hides his identity as a royal prince and works at her father’s fast-food restaurant to get closer to her. Will Akeem and Lisa fall in love as he cosplays being working class. Will Lisa leave her rich but arrogant fiance? Will their families accept their Lisa and Akeem if they do decide to marry? Spoiler alert: there’s a happy ending. The plot progression is simple but the character development is full of heart and candor.
text.alt_text: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie — The Guardian - Culture

audio.title: Your favorite apple is a cloned ovary – and other apple facts
audio.description: What’s your favorite apple? Whether it’s classic Gala, tart Granny Smith, the crowd-pleasing Honeycrisp or the infamous Red Delicious – before your favorite apple made it to your local orchard or your neighborhood grocery store, it had to be invented – by a scientist . So in this Short Wave episode, we’re going straight to the source. Host Emily Kwong and producer Hannah Chinn dive into how apples are selected, bred and grown, and discuss the discoveries that could change that process. Plus: What’s a spitter?

audio.title: Who were 'Churchill's Pirates'? (And how did they outfox Hitler?)
audio.description: They didn't wear uniforms. They sported grubby smocks and bandanas. They manned beaten-up old fishing trawlers that sometimes looked barely fit for sea. And yet members of the Royal Naval Patrol Service – otherwise known as 'Churchill's Pirates' – may well have been the difference between victory and defeat in the Second World War. In this episode, Will Iredale tells Spencer Mizen how a ragtag band of former fishermen and landlubbing conscripts helped stymie Hitler's plans to starve Britain into submission. ----- GO BEYOND THE PODCAST We’ve got a wealth of podcasts on the Second World War at sea available on the HistoryExtra website and app – including an interview with Roger Moorhouse on the brutality of the U-boat campaign.
